title: US Senate unanimously passes bipartisan resolution honoring American October 7 victims
body: The United States Senate unanimously passed a bipartisan resolution honoring the American citizens killed by Hamas on October 7, 2023, on Wednesday.The resolution, S.Res.938, lists out 40 of the 46 Americans killed on October 7, as well as the seven hostages who were successfully freed alive from Hamas captivity.In passing the resolution, the Senate resolved to honor and mourn the victims; express condolences to the victims' families; condemn Hamas and its affiliates; commend the US government for its role in freeing some of the hostages; urge the government to continue working to free US citizens held hostage across the world; and supports continued engagement by the US government with October 7 victims and their families.The resolution also directs the Senate to dispatch a copy of the resolution to the families of American October 7 victims.US has duty to secure justice for its people, senator saysFlorida Sen. Rick Scott, who cosponsored the resolution along with Jewish Nevada Sen. Jacky Rosen, celebrated its passing in the Senate.“Three years ago, the world watched in horror as Hamas terrorists massacred innocent civilians, including American citizens," the Republican senator said. "Families were torn apart, communities were decimated, and innocents, including babies and young children, were barbarically murdered. Americans were among the victims. There is no moral gray area here; Hamas is evil. Our country must protect our people and has a duty to secure justice for them. I was proud to work with Senator Rosen to honor the Americans whose lives were unjustly taken from them and the hostages who will spend the rest of their lives scarred by that tragic day.”Rosen also responded to the resolutions' passing, saying that "It is our responsibility to make sure the world never forgets the unspeakable violence carried out by Hamas terrorists on October 7, 2023 – the deadliest day for Jews since the Holocaust."The Democratic senator added that she introduced the bipartisan resolution "to honor the Americans who were killed on that day and those taken hostage by Hamas. It also honors the hostages' families, who demonstrated remarkable courage during a time of intense grief and anxiety by being steadfast and fierce advocates for the return of their loved ones. Today, nearly three years after the horror of October 7, we mark this tragic date and reaffirm our commitment to supporting the American victims and their families and all those held hostage around the world.”

title: Omani flydubai hijacking suspect held no second nationality, sources say – exclusive
body: The Omani co-pilot suspected of trying to hijack and crash a flydubai flight to Israel held no second nationality, sources with knowledge of the investigation told The Jerusalem Post on Friday.The disclosure addresses one of the questions raised after Wednesday's attack aboard Flight FZ1073 from Dubai to Tel Aviv: whether the suspect held citizenship in another country that could have explained his assignment to an Israel-bound flight.The aircraft made an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia, after the co-pilot allegedly stabbed the captain. Passengers subdued the attacker, and additional pilots traveling aboard the aircraft helped bring it down safely. “He has no other nationality,” a source said.The sources also said the bilateral aviation agreement between Israel and the United Arab Emirates did not stipulate that pilots operating flights between the two countries must be nationals of countries maintaining diplomatic relations with Israel.That account adds a new dimension to the dispute over how the Omani co-pilot was permitted to operate the flight. Oman does not have diplomatic relations with Israel, and the suspect's nationality was central to Transportation Minister Miri Regev's request on Wednesday to halt flydubai flights to and from the country. Questions over the conditions for flying to IsraelA Transportation Ministry source previously told the Post that flydubai's agreement to operate in Israel required pilots to be nationals of countries that had normalized relations with Israel.“This is a clear breach of the agreement,” the ministry source said at the time, calling for the Shin Bet, Israel's domestic security agency, to investigate. The sources' account on Friday concerned the bilateral aviation agreement. It did not address whether a separate operating or security arrangement imposed additional requirements on flydubai. Their description therefore does not, on its own, resolve whether the co-pilot's assignment violated the conditions governing the airline's flights to Israel.The sources provided no further information about the suspect's motives or possible connections to others.Pilot underwent radical Islamist indoctrination, Netanyahu revealsPrime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Thursday that the co-pilot had undergone radical Islamist indoctrination, while cautioning that final conclusions had not been reached. Israeli security officials told Reuters that the initial assessment was that he had acted alone, though the investigation remained ongoing. The UAE's attorney-general ordered prosecutors to investigate the incident, including whether it involved terrorist activity, advance planning or direction. The announcement also urged against drawing conclusions before investigators had established the facts. In a separate interview published by the Post on Thursday, an Israeli passenger identified as Tal described an interval during the confrontation when the cockpit was empty, and the aircraft was descending. He said he urged two additional pilots forward while other passengers fought the attacker. The precise sequence inside the cockpit and the duration of that interval have not been independently established by the Post.

title: U S Navy Signs 24 4B Standard Missile-6 Deal to Accelerate Missile Production
body:
The U.S. Navy has awarded Raytheon a contract worth up to $24.4 billion to accelerate production of the Standard Missile-6 (SM-6), a multi-mission, ship-launched weapon used for anti-air warfare, anti-surface warfare and terminal-phase ballistic missile defense.
The five-year agreement includes two additional option years and is intended to increase manufacturing throughput, expand industrial capacity and deliver cost savings through longer-term procurement.
The SM-6 is approximately 6.6 metres long, weighs about 1,500 kg, uses solid-fuel rocket propulsion and can exceed Mach 3. Depending on the variant and mission, its range is publicly reported at more than 240 km. The missile uses inertial, command and radar guidance, including active and semi-active radar homing, and is integrated with the U.S. Navy's Aegis combat system. It can engage aircraft and cruise missiles, intercept ballistic missiles in their terminal phase and attack surface targets.
The award is part of a broader U.S. effort to expand weapons production, replenish missile inventories and strengthen defense-industrial supply chains. It follows other major munitions agreements, including a recent Tomahawk award, providing defense contractors with longer-term demand intended to support workforce expansion, manufacturing investment and critical-component supply.

title: Indian flydubai pilot who opened cockpit door shares story with Prime Minister Narendra Modi
body: The Indian pilot of the recent flydubai flight which saw an attempted hijacking spoke to Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in a video call on Friday morning, sharing his account of the events.According to the wounded pilot, Capt. Smit Machchhar, he had opened the cockpit door while on the floor of the plane and actively being attacked by his Omani copilot."I was lying on the floor injured but I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside," he said.Machchhar added that, while he was fighting for his life, "I knew I was not going to let others die."According to several Indian news outlets, Machchhar is a Gujarati Indian from Mumbai. According to his LinkedIn profile, he spent over a decade flying for Indian airline SpiceJet, where he also served as a training captain and mentor for new pilots, before moving to flydubai. His profile also notes that he accumulated about 9,750 flying hours on the 737-800 and the 737 MAX 8 and 9.Israelis returned to Ben-Gurion Airport after attempted hijackingOne hundred and seventy-four Israeli passengers were returned to Ben-Gurion Airport Tuesday evening after multiple passengers helped restrain an Omani hijacker-pilot who attempted to crash the airplane earlier in the day.The passengers were initially on a flydubai commercial passenger aircraft flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv, but then the pilot-hijacker, who was the deputy pilot for the flight, stabbed the lead pilot and tried to crash the aircraft before as many as four passengers wounded him and tied him up.An additional flight crew on board were then able to handle landing the plane in Saudi Arabia, though the original pilot, Machchhar, was in critical condition, having been stabbed repeatedly by the Omani pilot.Maya Zanger-Shamir, Amichai Stein, Yonah Jeremy Bob, James Genn, and Zvika Klein contributed to this report.

title: Iran weighing options against US, Israel as nuclear talks stall, Israeli defense official says
body: Iran is weighing how to respond to growing US pressure as nuclear negotiations with Washington remain stalled, creating an increasingly complex regional situation, a senior Israeli defense official said on Friday."The Iranians are looking for tools within this campaign. They are asking themselves how they can get out of this situation. It is reasonable to assume that they are also discussing the possibility of influencing the elections in order to understand the other side," the official said.The senior defense official said there had recently been a large number of unresolved incidents, some of which could potentially develop into attacks on the Israeli home front from a variety of directions, and not necessarily from Iran."There were many warnings and many nights when the system was occupied with clarifying the situation and raising and lowering the alert level. There were many nights of heightened readiness. Hezbollah? It definitely factors into Iran's calculations if Iran enters into a confrontation with Israel," the official said.According to the defense official, the Iranians are constantly assessing the situation in the US and the extent of Washington's readiness to enter into a confrontation with them, and this affects Tehran's own assessment of the situation.Economic pressure mounts on IranThe official also stressed that conditions in Iran are deteriorating and that the effect of US sanctions can be clearly seen.The number of tankers leaving the Persian Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz has been rising, and according to IDF data, an average of 30 to 40 tankers are now passing through each day. That figure reflects levels seen before the war. In other words, Iranian influence in the strait is declining.The official also noted that the Iranian rial had reached a new low in recent days, with nearly 2.5 million rials now equivalent to one US dollar. At the same time, he clarified that Iran had not yet reached hyperinflation.The official illustrated the economic situation by citing a critical article in an Iranian newspaper identified with the regime that compared the price of eggs in Iran with the average salary, adding that the cost of living in Iran was now "unbearable."Compounding the economic pressure is what the official described as a US naval blockade of Iran that began this week. In addition to the sanctions, he said, the measure contains elements that are humiliating for Tehran because it prevents even family visits to neighboring countries.As a result, the Iranians quickly approached neighboring countries and asked them to restore civilian flights. So far, according to the official, only Iraq has agreed, while there are currently no flights with Azerbaijan.Israel prepares for risk of escalationIsraeli defense officials assess that Tehran is considering how to respond to the situation, what tools remain available to it, and what form its response should take. As evidence, they point to Iranian efforts to target vessels in the Strait of Hormuz that have so far failed.The defense establishment believes Iran's range of options has narrowed significantly because of the naval blockade. This comes alongside Iranian attempts to carry out attacks abroad that have also failed, according to the assessment.Israeli defense officials further assess that unless Iran attempts to break the blockade through a deliberate military move or reaches understandings with the US, it will be forced to contend with worsening domestic problems caused by the sanctions.The IDF is therefore preparing for the possibility that an Iranian initiative could spiral out of control, such as a cruise missile striking a US vessel and causing fatalities, creating a situation in which it would be unclear how Washington would respond.Israeli defense officials also assess that if the Iranians conclude that they are about to come under attack, or that the regime is losing ground in its confrontation with the US, they could potentially launch attacks against US assets in Jordan or Israel.A senior official said the Iranians understand very well what the price of such a move would be, and that this is why they have not attacked Israel.

title: El Al forced to cancel first rescue flights to Dubai after authorities revoke landing permissions
body: El Al Israel Airlines has been forced to cancel its rescue flights to Dubai, the company announced on Friday morning, after Israeli airlines' permission to land there was revoked by the authorities.El Al stated that, as soon as official permission is granted for the rescue flights to resume, it would be implementing the planned flights to bring stranded Israelis home.Meanwhile, the Transportation Ministry said that "following coordination with all relevant parties, it was agreed that flights operated by Israeli airlines from Dubai to Israel would begin on Friday, October 2. However, due to the need to complete the necessary preparations and coordination by security officials for the operation of the flights, a delay is expected in the departure of the repatriation flights from Dubai.“Citizens currently in Dubai should remain in contact with the airlines through which their tickets were booked and follow their instructions and updates,” the ministry added.According to estimates, more than 10,000 Israelis are stranded in Dubai and at other destinations from which they had been expected to return to Israel via the United Arab Emirates.Later on Friday, Israir announced that it had received the final approvals from the Emirati authorities and that flights would be departing from Israel to Dubai during the day. No similar announcement was made by El Al.Flydubai altercation leads to emergency landing in Saudi ArabiaOn Wednesday, a flydubai aircraft that departed Dubai for Tel Aviv was diverted and landed in Saudi Arabia following an altercation between the captain and the copilot.During the incident, one of them was stabbed, prompting the activation of the distress signal.The aircraft initially disappeared from flight tracking systems, raising concerns that it had been hijacked. However, after several tense moments, the circumstances surrounding the incident became clearer, and the plane made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

title: Government extends emergency reservist call-ups through November, lowers cap to 200,000
body: The government approved an extension on Wednesday of the emergency framework allowing the IDF to call up reservists under Order 8 through November 30, while reducing the maximum number of call-ups from 240,000 to 200,000, according to a proposal submitted by the Defense Ministry.Ministers approved two security-related decisions in a telephone vote. The first extends the authority to call reservists into service under Order 8. The second extends by two months the declaration allowing special arrangements for the detention of unlawful combatants.A legal opinion prepared by the defense establishment devoted considerable attention to the continuing toll on the reserve system. The decision, it said, raises "extremely significant difficulties regarding equality," since the burden on those who actually serve continues to increase while the state has not fulfilled its obligation to ensure equitable conscription across all sectors of the population.The opinion also noted that the government has not expanded the range of sanctions or sufficiently enforced conscription requirements against draft evaders. The result, according to the opinion, is a situation in which "with one hand the government increases the burden on reservists, and with the other it does not act to enforce the conscription obligation on draft evaders."Haredi conscription remains central to reserve burdenThe issue of haredi (ultra-Orthodox) conscription also features prominently in the explanation for the continuing need for reservists. According to the IDF's position, expanding the reserve system cannot replace fully utilizing the manpower available through mandatory service, which has a "dramatic impact" on force building.Call-up orders have been sent to draft-eligible members of the haredi public, and the IDF has stepped up enforcement against draft evaders, but the disparity in the distribution of the burden remains. Despite this, defense officials maintain that the security situation and the IDF's needs do not currently allow the military to end Order 8 reserve call-ups.In its explanatory notes, the Defense Ministry justified extending the order on the basis of continuing threats, IDF activity in multiple sectors, and operational requirements.The size of the call-up framework has changed several times over the course of the year. On March 24, amid Operation Roaring Lion and operations against Hezbollah and in other sectors, a framework of up to 400,000 reservists was approved through May 31.On July 26, a framework of up to 240,000 was approved through September 30. The proposal now approved by ministers will allow up to 200,000 reservist call-ups through November 30, a reduction of 40,000 from the framework expiring on September 30.The 200,000-call-up framework does not mean that 200,000 reservists may be serving simultaneously. Rather, it is the maximum number of reservist call-ups that may be issued under the order throughout the period.As a rule, a soldier who is released and subsequently called up again will be counted as an additional call-up, subject to exceptions stipulated in the order. Each call-up will take place only after the available standing forces have been fully utilized and will require individual approval from the head of the IDF Operations Division's Operations Brigade or the official responsible for recruitment and readiness within the brigade.Nearly three years after October 7, the exceptional use of Order 8 remains necessary, according to the Defense Ministry, because the statutory limitations on reserve service do not allow the IDF to maintain the required force levels for extended periods.Under the ordinary legal framework, the maximum number of reserve-duty days over a three-year period is 54 days for enlisted personnel, 70 days for commanders, and 84 days for officers. Operational duty may ordinarily be performed once every three years for a period of up to 25 days.The proposal states that Israel's security needs require maintaining significant troop levels in various sectors for far longer periods, necessitating the continued use of Order 8 call-ups.The proposal also details steps taken to increase the manpower available to the IDF and ease the burden. Tens of thousands of reservists have been returned from manpower pools to active units, reserve exemptions have been canceled for thousands of soldiers, and the reserve exemption age has been raised to 49 in certain essential professions and units.In July, a temporary provision stipulated that mandatory service would remain 32 months and would not be shortened to 30 months over the next three years. The defense establishment had originally sought to extend men's mandatory service to 36 months, but the Knesset approved only part of the measure.According to data attached to the proposal, the total cost of reserve-duty days carried out under Order 8 from January through August stood at NIS 26.7 billion, while the average cost of one day of reserve duty under Order 8 is estimated at approximately NIS 1,000.The estimated cost of the proposed extension is based on the average volume of reserve-duty days between January and September. If that level continues through October and November, the estimated cost of the additional two months will be approximately NIS 6.6 billion.Government also extends unlawful combatant detention frameworkThe second decision submitted for ministers' approval extends the declaration under the Incarceration of Unlawful Combatants Law. The current declaration expires on September 30, and the government sought to extend it through November 30.The extension means that the special arrangements introduced during the war regarding the detention of unlawful combatants will remain in force. These include the amount of time allowed before issuing a permanent detention order, the possibility of preventing a detainee from meeting with a lawyer, and the timetable for judicial review.The ceasefire was signed in October 2025 and intensive ground maneuvers in the Gaza Strip were halted, but according to the Defense Ministry, conditions on the ground still justify extending the declaration.IDF troops remain in enemy territory, friction continues in various sectors, and dozens of people suspected of involvement in terrorism continue to be detained. Thousands of unlawful combatants remain in detention, including detainees for whom permanent detention orders have not yet been issued and others who have been prevented from meeting with a lawyer.The legal opinion stated that repeatedly extending the declaration "is not a trivial matter." The number of new detainees has fallen, the ceasefire has already entered into effect, and terrorist organizations in the Gaza Strip no longer hold hostages.Defense officials argue, however, that the IDF remains active on several fronts and that some detainees undergo complex investigations during which it is sometimes necessary to prevent them from meeting with a lawyer.If the declaration expires, existing decisions preventing detainees from meeting with lawyers would expire immediately. In some cases, authorities would be required to issue a permanent detention order and bring the detainee before a court for judicial review before the investigation had been completed and the necessary factual basis had been established.Against this background, the legal opinion concluded that although another extension presents difficulties, there is no legal impediment to approving it.The arrangements currently in force are already narrower than those applied during earlier stages of the war. Under the latest amendment to the temporary provision, which entered into effect on July 1, a permanent detention order for an unlawful combatant must be signed within 18 days of detention, or within 10 days in the case of a minor.The periods before judicial review were shortened by seven days, and the maximum periods during which a detainee may be prevented from meeting with a lawyer were also reduced.The Defense Ministry stressed that these are maximum periods and that, in practice, efforts are made to shorten them in accordance with the security situation and the number of new detainees.Both decisions are being made during an election period, when the government is subject to a heightened duty of restraint. The legal opinions determined that the decisions are urgent, security-related, and limited in duration, and are required because the two existing arrangements expire on September 30.The opinions therefore concluded that there is no legal impediment to approving them during the election period.

title: Bill on national minority education rights registered in Rada to lift Hungary's veto on opening negotiation clusters
body:
Members of the Verkhovna Rada have registered a bill on education for national minorities aimed at unblocking the opening of two negotiation clusters regarding Ukraine's accession to the European Union by lifting Hungary's veto.
"We have found a solution that simultaneously protects the Ukrainian language, grants clear rights to national minorities and indigenous peoples, and removes one of the obstacles to Ukraine's European integration, specifically, it will help us unblock the opening of two negotiation clusters by lifting Hungary's veto," wrote Serhiy Babak (Servant of the People faction), head of the Verkhovna Rada Committee on Education, Science, and Innovation, on his Telegram channel.
Specifically, the measure in question is Bill No. 16119, "On amendments to certain laws of Ukraine regarding ensuring the right to education for indigenous peoples of Ukraine and persons belonging to national minorities (communities) of Ukraine."
Babak emphasized that the Ukrainian language remains the language of the educational process, and the bill neither diminishes its status nor reintroduces the Russian language into the education system.
"It is about something else. We need to regulate the right to education for Ukraine's indigenous peoples and national minorities whose languages ​​are official languages ​​of the European Union, while simultaneously fulfilling a crucial part of our European integration commitments," he added.
According to him, the bill is intended to create the necessary conditions for further unblocking the negotiation process, particularly regarding the next two clusters.
"At the outset, our negotiating position was far from simple. The groundwork and agreements established by those previously responsible for this process had effectively led the discussion into a dead end. Furthermore, the version of the bill they had agreed to would not have garnered sufficient support even within the relevant committee, let alone on the floor of the Verkhovna Rada. Yet, politics is the art of reaching agreements while upholding one's state's position," the MP wrote.
The committee chair noted that the bill more clearly defines how the languages ​​of Ukraine's indigenous peoples and national minorities, specifically those that are official EU languages, may be used alongside the state language.
"For instance, if an educational institution has a class where children are taught in Hungarian, they will be able to use the language of an EU country (alongside Ukrainian) not only during instruction but also when communicating with teachers and other participants in the educational process. Ukrainian remains the state language of instruction, and these changes apply exclusively to the languages ​​of European Union countries," he wrote.
The bill also introduces the concept of a general secondary education institution with the status of a national minority (or community) institution; to qualify for this status, an institution must have more than 50% of its students (specifically, 50% plus one) studying in the language of that national minority (or community).
"According to Ministry of Education and Science estimates, this potentially affects 149 educational institutions—about 1.2% of all general secondary education institutions in Ukraine. In other words, we are talking about a very specific and rather limited group of institutions, and certainly not a change to the overall language model of education in Ukraine," Babak emphasized.
Furthermore, according to the draft document, parents will be able to initiate an expansion of the list of subjects taught in Ukrainian. In other words, if a child is studying in a class or group where the language of instruction is that of an indigenous people or a national minority, provided that language is an official EU language, the number of subjects taught in Ukrainian may be increased.
Among other things, the requirement regarding language certification is changing for the heads of certain private educational institutions.
"This provision applies to a very narrow group of heads of private educational institutions (specifically, those serving as heads at the time the law enters into force) that have classes or groups where the educational process is conducted in the language of an indigenous people or a national minority that is an official EU language. They will not be required to provide a state certificate confirming their Ukrainian language proficiency for as long as they remain in their position," the message reads.
According to the Ministry of Education, this affects the heads of only 29 institutions across Ukraine.
"That is why I would very much dislike seeing the discussion around this bill reduced to a simplistic 'Ukrainian language versus minority languages' confrontation. We have actually found a solution that ensures the rights of national minorities without compromising the position of the Ukrainian language. We are fulfilling our obligations to the citizens of Ukraine and continuing our progress toward European Union membership," Babak stated.
The bill's authors include Ruslan Stefanchuk, Oleksandr Kornienko, Olena Kondratiuk, Serhiy Babak, Mykyta Poturayev, Oleksandr Danutsa, Yevhenia Kravchuk, Serhiy Kalchenko, Andriy Klochko, Oleksandr Horobets, Dmytro Liubota, Mykola Davydiuk, Vadym Halaichuk, and Maria Mezentseva-Fedorenko.
As reported, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha expressed hope for the early convening of a special session of the Verkhovna Rada to consider a package of documents on European integration and a bill on national minorities.

title: Russia lost 2026-record 46,230 troops in September by Ukraine’s count, as fighting around Donetsk fortress cities grinds on
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Russia lost more troops in September than in any other month this year, hitting the record, by Ukraine's count. The General Staff put last month's Russian casualties at 46,230, a 2026 record and 45.8% above January's. At the same time, Russia's strikes on Ukraine's rear escalated in September and are climbing again in October. The result is a grind that bleeds Russia on the ground while Ukrainian cities absorb the blows from above. Losses span the whole front "Ukraine's Defense Forces continue to inflict systemic and tangible losses on the Russian occupation forces in personnel and equipment along the entire line of contact," the General Staff says. The toll climbs all year The monthly figures have risen almost without pause. After a dip to 26,090 in February, Russian losses climbed through the spring and summer, 39,290 in June, 42,860 in July, 42,020 in August, before last month's high. The record reaches down to a single day: the General Staff counted 2,090 Russian casualties in the 24 hours to 28 September, which British Defense Intelligence assessed as the highest daily toll since the full-scale invasion, one of only four days to top 2,000, the other three in 2024. British intelligence tied the high rate to intense fighting around the fortified belt of Donetsk cities, especially near Dobropillia. Meanwhile, Kyiv is also continuing its Vivaldi Operation near Lyman, and its latest mission used ground robots, each carrying two Bullspike grenade launchers to launch an attack on Russian positions and then detonate inside their shelters. Kyiv reads the climb Across the war, Ukraine says it has put roughly 1.5 million Russian troops out of action, a toll that has bought little ground as the months-long summer offensive stalled short of its goals. "Every attempt to pressure our positions ends for the enemy in disproportionate losses of wounded and killed," the General Staff says. The figures are Kyiv's own and cannot be independently checked: they count the Russians' wounded and killed but never their own. title: Ukraine Claims First Combat Use Of FP-7 Ballistic Missile
body: Ukraine says it has used its domestically developed FP-7 tactical ballistic missile in combat for the first time, in what would mark another significant milestone in the country’s rapidly expanding indigenous long-range strike program . President Volodymyr Zelensky announced today that Ukraine had conducted the first combat use of the FP-7, a ground-launched ballistic missile developed by Ukrainian defense company Fire Point . He also said production of the weapon would follow. Ukrainian tactical ballistic missile. FP-7. First combat use. Thank you for the result. Next up: production. Glory to Ukraine! pic.twitter.com/IxdjVg51c1 — Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) October 1, 2026 The claim has not been independently verified, and Ukrainian authorities have not disclosed the target, location, number of missiles involved, or other details surrounding the reported strike. A video has been published showing what’s said to be a nighttime launch of the missile. The FP-7 is one of several increasingly ambitious weapons being developed by Fire Point, a Ukrainian defense company that has expanded rapidly since Russia’s full-scale invasion. The company began with drones and has subsequently moved into long-range strike missiles and ballistic missile technology. Test launch of the FP-7 surface-to-surface ballistic missile. Fire Point Fire Point CEO Iryna Terekh previously described the company’s development and manufacturing model in an interview with TWZ , detailing an effort to rapidly scale production while maintaining a dispersed industrial base inside Ukraine. The company’s better-known systems include the FP-1 and FP-2 long-range strike drones and the FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile . According to Ukrainian and company-released information, the FP-7 has a range of approximately 250 kilometers (155 miles) and a warhead weighing around 150 kilograms (331 pounds). Other published figures have put its velocity at approximately 1,500 meters per second (around 3,350 miles per hour). Rather than striking targets deep in the Russian rear areas, the missile is optimized for use against objectives such as logistics hubs, air defense sites, and drone bases. This makes it more of a shorter-range complement to the U.S.-supplied Army Tactical Missile System (ATACMS) ballistic missile, rather than a direct replacement, although it comes without any restrictions on the kinds of targets that it can be used against. Details from missile debris shown by Russia confirm Ukraine launched ATACMS at Voronezh region on November 18, marking the first use of U.S.-made missiles on Russian territory during Trump’s presidency. According to the Russian MoD, S-400 and Pantsir-S1 systems helped repel the… pic.twitter.com/8SeQCo9OEO — NOELREPORTS (@NOELreports) November 19, 2025 At the same time, those specifications should likewise be treated as reported figures rather than independently verified performance data. Actual range, payload and accuracy can vary according to missile configuration and mission profile. The FP-7’s development is particularly notable because Fire Point is also using the basic missile architecture as the foundation for a very different weapon. Fire Point has developed the FP-7.X, an anti-ballistic missile interceptor derived from the surface-to-surface FP-7. A video showing a test launch of an FP-7.X surface-to-air missile: Держави програють війни на полі бою значно рідше, ніж вони програють їх у інститутах, лабораторіях та на виробництві за десять років до їх початку. Коли країна роками недофінансовує інженерну освіту, скорочує дослідження, втрачає виробничі компетенції або звикає покладатися на… pic.twitter.com/Ti1Ayn4INf — terekh (@iraterekh) June 3, 2026 Fire Point’s expectation is that commonality between the two systems can shorten development and provide manufacturing efficiencies by allowing the company to draw upon work already conducted on the FP-7’s propulsion, airframe, guidance, and production processes. The FP-7.X forms part of Project Freyja , a European effort to develop a comparatively inexpensive and potentially more numerous ballistic-missile-defense interceptor. Fire Point has also discussed an eventual production rate of thousands of interceptors annually, although such targets represent company ambitions rather than demonstrated production capacity. Fire Point has said it is working with European and Ukrainian partners on the system, including work on the interceptor’s seeker. The company has described an initial interceptor using a blast-fragmentation approach, with more sophisticated hit-to-kill capability envisioned for later versions. Earlier this year, Diehl Defense confirmed that it plans to launch production of the Flamingo cruise missile in Germany. Previously, Diehl had signed a technology agreement with Fire Point but had not disclosed any details. Potentially, that could open a path to Fire Point’s ballistic and cruise missiles helping to meet the growing demand for long-range fires capabilities among NATO’s European members. A video of the Flamingo cruise missile in action: As it stands, the baseline FP-7 is only one element of Fire Point’s ballistic missile ambitions. A rendering of the FP-7 surface-to-surface ballistic missile. Fire Point The company is also developing the larger FP-9, which Fire Point has described as having a planned range of approximately 850 kilometers (528 miles). The larger missile requires substantially more solid propellant and has driven the company to establish new industrial capabilities for manufacturing large solid-rocket motors. As with the FP-7, the available FP-9 performance figures are based primarily on statements from Fire Point and Ukrainian sources and should not be treated as independently established specifications. The development of these weapons reflects Ukraine’s broader effort to expand domestic production of long-range strike systems. Kyiv has relied heavily on Western-supplied weapons during the war while simultaneously attempting to establish an indigenous capacity for drones, cruise missiles, and ballistic missiles. For Fire Point, that effort has produced an unusually broad portfolio in a relatively short period: long-range attack drones, cruise missiles, ballistic missiles and, potentially, interceptors designed to defeat ballistic missiles. The claimed combat debut would give Ukraine a fast, hard-to-intercept strike option for targets within the FP-7’s reported range, with its combination of kinetic energy and relatively heavy warhead making it particularly useful against hardened targets. If targeting and launch procedures can keep pace, its short flight time can also enable rapid-response strikes against more time-sensitive targets. More broadly, the FP-7 represents the culmination of years of Ukrainian efforts to close a major ballistic-missile gap with Russia and establish an indigenous capability. FP-7 surface-to-surface ballistic missile. Fire Point The reported combat debut of the FP-7 also comes as the long-range strike campaign between Russia and Ukraine continues to intensify, with both sides increasingly seeking to hold targets deep behind the other’s front lines at risk. That dynamic will become particularly important as the two countries head into another winter, when strikes against energy, industrial, and military infrastructure ramp up significantly. At the same time, the FP-7’s reported range gives it a considerably more limited target set than Ukraine’s longer-range cruise missiles and drones, constraining where it can be employed and distinguishing it from systems designed for deep strikes hundreds of miles beyond the front. Вітаємо FP7) pic.twitter.com/FxgCHVHMET — Denys Shtilierman (@DenShtilierman) February 27, 2026 The significance of Zelensky’s announcement will ultimately depend heavily on whether the FP-7 can move from a claimed combat debut into sustained production and operational service. Ukraine has not publicly disclosed the number of FP-7 missiles produced, current production rates, or when significant quantities could become available. Using the FP-7 in combat for the first time would mark an important transition for Fire Point’s ballistic missile program, from development and testing toward operational employment. The company’s ability to manufacture the weapon at scale will become the next critical question. title: Ukrainian firm fields 11 crewless boats and eight drones at NATO’s biggest naval drone drill
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); UFORCE, a Ukrainian defense company, says it fielded 11 crewless boats and eight drones at NATO's largest unmanned-systems exercise in Portugal, Militarnyi reported . The firm's crews acted as both mock enemy and allied forces alongside Ukraine's Navy during the 31 August–25 September drills. The turnout more than doubled the company's presence at last year's exercise, when it brought five vessels. Ukraine began the all-out war without large warships, yet uncrewed boats drove Russia's Black Sea Fleet out of its main base on the Black Sea—a result that now pulls far larger navies to the same ranges to test the weapon for themselves. Ukraine brings its sea-drone playbook to Portugal's NATO exercise UFORCE joined REPMUS 26, the Portuguese Navy's annual exercise, co-organized with NATO, where member states try out robots and drones built for combat at sea. This year the company widened its presence sharply, UFORCE said on LinkedIn. Across the scenarios, its crews ran strikes, reconnaissance, and defense. At the center sat the MV7, an uncrewed boat UFORCE showed in every setup it offers. Across its configurations, the MV7 carried interceptors, FPV drones, other kinetic weapons, and electronic-warfare gear. Crews launched flying drones straight off the decks while the boats sat on the water, all run by a single control program. The company brought three systems to REPMUS for the first time: the Nemesis SeaStrike drone, which launches from the MV7, the MV11 boat, and a supply vessel called L11. UFORCE teams worked beside Ukraine's Navy throughout. Portuguese President António José Seguro inspected the MV7 on the pier, the company said. Not Ukraine's first visit Ukraine was at REPMUS last year, too. At REPMUS 2025, a Ukrainian-led "enemy" team beat NATO's side across all five drill scenarios and, in one, landed enough mock strikes on a NATO frigate to have sunk it in a real battle. Ukraine also brought the upgraded Magura v7.2 to that year's drills. Read also Ukraine’s new ground robot switches from land to water in seconds. title: F-22 Pilots Awarded Distinguished Flying Cross for Actions in CENTCOM, Including Midnight Hammer
body: Seven F-22 Raptor pilots have recently been awarded one of the military’s highest decorations for their actions during operations in the Middle East. Six of the pilots were decorated with the Distinguished Flying Cross for their role in Operation Midnight Hammer , the June 2025 strikes against Iranian nuclear facilities Another pilot currently stationed in Europe received a DFC for a mission in the Middle East, but the Air Force did not say when or where the actions that earned that pilot the award occurred. The six Airmen from Langley were decorated for their actions escorting B-2 Spirit stealth bombers that struck the Fordow and Natanz nuclear sites in Iran. The strike package also included F-16 Fighting Falcons and F-35 Lightning II fighters, and pilots from those units received DFCs earlier this year; tanker crews from multiple units have also received the award for supporting the mission. No individual awards have yet been announced for the B-2 aviators who participated in Midnight Hammer. The DFC recognizes acts of heroism or extraordinary achievement in the air and is the military’s fourth-highest award for heroism. Four of the pilots came from the Active-Duty 94th Fighter Squadron, part of the 1st Fighter Wing at Joint Base Langley-Eustis, Va., and two pilots came from the associated Virginia Air National Guard’s 149th Fighter Squadron, part of the 192nd Wing. The medals were presented Aug. 31 by the head of Air Combat Command, Gen. Adrian L. Spain, in a ceremony at the Virginia base. Distinguished Flying Cross medals with the “C” device wait to be presented at Quesada Hall, Langley Air Force Base, Va., Aug. 31, 2026. U.S. Air Force photo by Airman 1st Class Kaden Ciminnisi The F-22s were among an armada of fighters that escorted the seven B-2s that dropped 14 30,000-pound GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator weapons on Iran’s nuclear facilities. Around 125 U.S. aircraft of all types were involved in the mission, which came after a nearly two-week Israeli air campaign against Iran. The stealthy F-22s serve as the Air Force’s premier air-to-air fighters and can use their capabilities to penetrate defended airspace. “Their job was to provide air superiority,” Spain said, according to an account of his remarks provided by the 1st Fighter Wing. “The bombers and the rest of the support package relied on these Raptor pilots to clear the skies, shield them from surface threats, and ensure a safe route through heavily contested airspace.” Officials from Air Combat Command and the 1st Fighter Wing declined to provide further details on the mission that earned the pilots their decorations or medal citations, or to publicly disclose pilots’ identities, citing operational security concerns. “We haven’t awarded many of these in the last few decades, as it’s intended to recognize true heroism and highly exceptional accomplishment in flight, which means that it should be rare, and it is,” said Spain. U.S. Air Force Gen. Adrian Spain, commander of Air Combat Command, stands at attention during the ruffles and flourishes prior to a Distinguished Flying Cross presentation ceremony at Quesada Hall, Langley Air Force Base, Va., Aug. 31, 2026. U.S. Air Force photo by Airman 1st Class Kaden Ciminnisi Iran’s air force was largely destroyed during the 2026 air campaign against the country, Operation Epic Fury. But even during Midnight Hammer, Iran posed a limited air-to-air threat, with most of its capability consisting of aircraft purchased before the Iranian revolution in 1979. Before the Shah was overthrown and a theocratic government took over, Iran was the largest purchaser of American arms. Iran also has Soviet-designed fighters. Still, Iran showed the ability to generate some airpower, launching aircraft to attack Gulf countries after Israel and Iran began their air campaign on Feb. 28 of this year, and was able to strike a base in Kuwait used by the U.S. with one of its aging fighter jets. F-22s from Langley deployed to support Operation Epic Fury and follow-on actions against Iran earlier this year but have since returned. A U.S. Air Force F-22 Raptor aircraft takes flight during Operation Epic Fury, March 20, 2026. U.S. Air Force photo “It was your support that enabled their excellence—from the maintainers, the operations team, the intel professionals, and the logistics involved,” Spain said. “Let there be no doubt heroism like this is earned by the entire formation. These pilots were the leading edge that day, but the foundation of their success was laid by the hard work of the entire organization in the days prior and every day since. And that’s what Air Force readiness looks like.” The seventh F-22 pilot received their decoration Sept. 22 from U.S. Air Forces in Europe commander Lt. Gen. Jason T. Hinds for leading a strike package during a mission in the Middle East that operated in contested airspace, according to a release from the command. U.S. officials did not immediately say whether the mission was part of Operation Epic Fury, Operation Midnight Hammer, or Operation Rough Rider , the 2025 campaign against the Houthis in Yemen. U.S. Air Force Lt. Gen. Jason T. Hinds, U.S. Air Forces in Europe – U.S. Air Forces Africa commander, speaks during a Distinguished Flying Cross award presentation in Essen, Germany, Sept. 22, 2026. U.S. Navy photo by Mass Communication Specialist 2nd Class Samuel Wagner The pilot faced “challenging conditions including enemy threats” and “directed the aircraft formation, making critical decisions with limited time and little margin for error,” according to USAFE. The command, like ACC, withheld the Airman’s identity. “For more than an hour, [the pilot] remained focused on protecting teammates” and “acted decisively to protect the larger force, and ensured the formation could safely return,” Hinds said. “Their actions helped give the strike package the time and freedom needed to accomplish its mission.” The post F-22 Pilots Awarded Distinguished Flying Cross for Actions in CENTCOM, Including Midnight Hammer appeared first on Air & Space Forces Magazine .

title: Spain, Belgium, and Poland are sending Ukraine F-16 cannon rounds to fight Russia’s jet drones
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Ukraine may soon receive a multimillion package of 20-mm rounds for its F-16 fighter jets, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha told journalists, Hromadske reported . He called the ammunition critical for shooting down Russia's jet-powered drones and said several partners have already begun transferring it. He expects the larger package after an upcoming high-level visit. Russia now strikes Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities daily, increasingly with jet-powered drones that outrun the cheap interceptors built for slower Shaheds. Fighter jets are among the tools Ukraine uses against them, while its overall interception rate for jet drones still trails its rate against propeller drones. "Critically important" ammunition Sybiha said Ukraine has yet to build up its capability to repel jet drones. "Given that we have not yet built up the capability to repel jet drones, and given the preparations for new strikes, it was critically important to help our military shoot down these drones. Apart from air defense systems, which are too expensive to use constantly against drones, the most effective tools right now are F-16 fighter jets," Sybiha said. He thanked Spain, Belgium, and Poland, which have begun the process of transferring the ammunition, and said that thanks to them Ukraine will "very soon" have the rounds it needs. Explore further Belgium will send three F-16 fighter jets, but maintenance delays may keep Ukraine from using them A "very serious visit" ahead Sybiha linked the larger package to a visit he did not name. "We will soon have one very serious visit. We think that one of the decisions following this visit will be a multimillion package of this ammunition for Ukraine," he said. Talks on buying the rounds from private manufacturers are also underway, he added. Ukraine has already received urgent batches of F-16 ammunition from Belgium, Spain, and other partners, and Belgium plans to send three more F-16s by the end of 2026 under an accelerated procedure. The jets' air-to-air missiles and cannon rounds are imported and not always in stock. Explore further Combat shows speed alone can’t catch Russia’s jet-powered drones, despite eight Ukrainian makers’ assurances. So why can’t they stop them? Another night of Russian strikes Overnight on 2 October, Russia launched 108 drones at Ukraine, 47 of them jet-powered, and air defenses downed 88 of them. In Kyiv, a Russian strike on a 25-story residential building in the Darnytskyi district killed one person and injured two. Russia also targeted the Southern Bridge again, after striking it three times the previous day, and the city restricted public transport across several bridges. In Kharkiv Oblast, a Russian FPV drone hit a car in the Solonytsivka hromada on the afternoon of 1 October, injuring a man and a boy. A Russian strike damaged a civilian enterprise in Rivne Oblast and started a fire that forced an evacuation of nearby homes, regional head Oleksandr Koval said, and drones attacked Cherkasy Oblast. In neighboring Romania, an object believed to be a drone crashed near the village of Plauru in Tulcea County during the attack, starting a fire that caused no casualties, Romania's Defense Ministry said . title: Greece is keeping its Patriot missiles in Saudi Arabia for one more month
body: Greece will keep its Patriot battery in Saudi Arabia for another month, Defence Minister Nikos Dendias said after a meeting of the Government Council for Foreign Affairs and Defence (KYSEA). “We will grant a one-month extension. I believe the issue with Saudi Arabia will be resolved,” Dendias told reporters as he left the Maximos Mansion. KYSEA decided the battery at Yanbu stays in place for that extra month. The Greek force in Saudi Arabia (ELDYSA) is there to help defend energy infrastructure that Yemen’s Houthis have repeatedly attacked. Dendias also said contracts for the “modern fighter” programme are moving ahead. Foreign Minister Giorgos Gerapetritis briefed the council on the Eastern Mediterranean, the Middle East and Ukraine, and on Greece’s agenda as it takes the presidency of the UN Security Council, government spokesman Pavlos Marinakis said. The session also covered deployments of Greek forces under international commitments.
